Malaria: Public Health Awareness Guide
A simple reference for community health awareness (for use by health awareness chatbots and community health workers)
Overview
Malaria is a serious illness spread by the bite of an infected mosquito. It is caused by a tiny parasite, not by a virus or bacteria, and it does not spread from one person to another through touch or air. Malaria is common in many warm, tropical parts of the world, including large parts of India, and it can affect people of any age. The good news is that malaria can be prevented and, if caught early, can be fully cured with proper medical treatment. Left untreated, however, malaria can become severe and even life-threatening, especially in young children, pregnant women, and people with weak immunity. Early recognition of symptoms and prompt treatment at a health facility are the most important steps in preventing serious illness or death from malaria.
Common Symptoms
Malaria symptoms usually appear about one to two weeks after the bite of an infected mosquito, though in some cases it can take longer. Common symptoms include:
Sudden high fever, often with shivering and chills
Heavy sweating as the fever breaks
Headache and body aches
Nausea and vomiting
Tiredness and weakness
Loss of appetite
A common pattern in malaria is a fever cycle: the person may first feel cold and shiver, then develop a high fever, and later sweat heavily as the fever comes down. This cycle may repeat every day or every few days depending on the type of malaria. Because early symptoms are similar to common flu or viral fever, malaria can be easily missed unless a blood test is done. Anyone with fever in a malaria-prone area should get tested rather than assume it is an ordinary fever.
Causes
Malaria is caused by a microscopic parasite that spreads through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. These mosquitoes are most active at night and during dusk and dawn hours. They breed in stagnant water found in ponds, puddles, paddy fields, ditches, and other water collections, especially in forested, hilly, and rural areas. When an infected mosquito bites a person, the parasite enters the bloodstream and multiplies in the liver before affecting the red blood cells, which is what causes fever and other symptoms. Malaria does not spread through coughing, touching, or sharing food or water with an infected person; it spreads only through the bite of an infected mosquito, and in rare cases through infected blood transfusions or contaminated needles.
When to See a Doctor (Warning Signs – Act Immediately)
Any fever in a malaria-prone area should be checked by a health worker or doctor with a blood test as soon as possible, since early diagnosis and treatment give the best outcome. Go to a doctor or hospital immediately, without delay, if the person has any of the following warning signs:
High fever that does not come down or keeps returning
Repeated vomiting, unable to keep fluids down
Extreme weakness or inability to stand or walk
Confusion, drowsiness, or difficulty staying awake
Convulsions or fits
Fast or difficult breathing
Yellowing of the eyes or skin (jaundice)
Very pale skin, palms, or eyes (signs of severe anaemia)
Dark or reduced urine output
Children under five, pregnant women, elderly people, and those with other health conditions are at higher risk of the illness turning severe quickly, so they should be taken for testing and treatment at the very first sign of fever rather than waiting to see if it improves on its own.
Home Care and Prevention
Home care (only for confirmed mild malaria under medical guidance):
Take complete rest and avoid strenuous work until fully recovered
Drink plenty of fluids – water, ORS, coconut water, or soup – to prevent dehydration
Eat light, nutritious food to support recovery
Take all medicines exactly as prescribed by the doctor, and complete the full course even if feeling better – stopping early can cause the illness to return or become harder to treat
Keep monitoring body temperature and overall condition, and return to the health centre if symptoms worsen
Prevention (avoiding mosquito bites and breeding):
Sleep under a mosquito net every night, especially insecticide-treated nets, even during the day for infants and young children
Use mosquito repellents and wear full-sleeved clothes, particularly in the evening and at night
Keep doors and windows screened or closed around dusk
Drain or treat stagnant water near homes, including puddles, ditches, and unused containers
Support local indoor residual spraying and larvicide programmes conducted by health workers
Get tested promptly for any fever, and inform the nearest health worker or ASHA if fever persists
Odisha-Specific Notes
Odisha has historically been among the states in India most affected by malaria, with the burden concentrated in specific parts of the state rather than spread evenly. Several tribal and forested districts, particularly in the southern, western, and northern belts of Odisha, have long recorded a higher number of malaria cases compared to the coastal districts. These areas tend to have hilly, forested terrain, scattered and remote habitations, and a warm, humid climate, all of which favour mosquito breeding and make regular healthcare access more difficult for some communities.
Because of this pattern, the state government and national health programmes have run focused malaria control and elimination efforts in these high-burden tribal and forested districts, including distribution of insecticide-treated mosquito nets, indoor spraying, and community-based screening and treatment camps carried out with the help of local health workers and ASHAs. Residents of these regions, and anyone travelling to or working in forested and rural parts of Odisha, should take mosquito bite prevention seriously and seek prompt testing for any fever rather than waiting, since early detection greatly improves treatment outcomes. Continued community participation in net use, water management, and reporting of fever cases remains central to reducing malaria's impact in these regions.
Source Basis
This document is based on general public health guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO), India's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) and its National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP), the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), and published research on malaria patterns in Odisha. It has been written in simple language for general awareness and paraphrased in the writer's own words; it is not a verbatim reproduction of any single source, and no specific statistics have been quoted.
Sources referred to:
World Health Organization (WHO) – www.who.int
Pan American Health Organization (PAHO/WHO) – www.paho.org
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India (MoHFW) / National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) – ncvbdc.mohfw.gov.in
Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
National Health Mission (NHM), Government of India
Government of Odisha, Department of Health and Family Welfare – health.odisha.gov.in
Peer-reviewed studies on malaria epidemiology and control in Odisha (published via PubMed/PMC, including work on the DAMaN programme and district-level surveillance)
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
